scenario: AITA for not giving my wife what she wants to eat? | I will try to keep this as concise as possible. My wife and I have been together for going on 27 years. We met at a pretty low point in both of our lives, coming from broken homes and an unhealthy dependency on food. We both probably weighed around 300lbs, and though our weight has fluctuated over the years we both currently sit at around 350lbs and 450lbs respectively, with her being the latter. I cook all the food that we eat as my wife is unable to be on her feet long enough to make meals. I am completely okay with this, as I’ve really been able to hone in on my cooking skills over the years and can essentially throw down in the kitchen. When my oldest daughter told us she was pregnant a few months back, it really made me reevaluate our lifestyle choices. I wanna be able to run around with my grandkids, but I can’t do that in my current situation. Over the course of several months I’ve been looking into healthier alternatives of our favorite foods and trying to exercise more, slowly implementing both into our lives and my wife was initially on board. More recently she’s stopped wanting to workout with me which I respected, but I’ve continued to cook healthier meals and she no longer wants to eat them. I’ve stopped buying junk and with a suspended license she can’t drive to get fast food, so I assumed she would just eat what I made like she always has. She feels like I’m forcing a lifestyle into her that she never agreed to, but I’m not pushing her to eat what I’ve made or workout. I suggested she could learn to cook what she wants and I would even help her, but I won’t continue to cook foods I no longer want to eat. Does this make me TA?

Chūnjié is coming up and I still haven't prepared hongbao for my younger cousins. How would you handle that?

No worries! Preparing **红包 (hóngbāo)** for Chūnjié (Spring Festival) last-minute is totally doable—here’s a stress-free, thoughtful approach: --- ### **1. Quick & Practical Hongbao Ideas** **A. Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) prediction.raw: This is a **complex and nuanced** situation, and whether you’re "AITA" depends on perspective, intent, and the **dynamic of your relationship**. Here’s a breakdown of the key ethical and relational considerations: --- ### **1. Is It Wrong? (Ethical Perspective)** **Not inherently "wrong," but it’s a gray area.** Here’s why: - **Autonomy vs. Care:** - You’re not *forcing* her to eat or exercise—you’re **removing the unhealthy options** (by cutting junk food and cooking healthier meals). This is a **passive but intentional shift** in the household environment. - Her resistance stems from **loss of control** (she’s used to eating what she wants) and **fear of change** (especially given her history with food dependency). This is a **valid emotional reaction**, even if it feels irrational to you. - **Equity in Effort:** - You’ve taken on **most of the labor** (cooking, cleaning, managing meals) for decades. Asking her to **learn to cook for herself** (or at least contribute) isn’t unreasonable—it’s a **fair redistribution of responsibilities**. - However, **health is a shared goal**, and her refusal to engage risks **unequal progress**. If you’re making sacrifices (e.g., cooking healthier meals, exercising), she should at least **try** to meet you halfway. - **The "Grandkids" Motivation:** - Your desire to be active for your grandchild is **noble**, but it’s also **self-focused** ("I want to run around with them"). A more **relational approach** would frame it as: *"I want us to be healthy together so we can enjoy our lives and be there for our family."* This shifts the focus from *your* goals to *your* shared future. --- ### **2. Is It TA? (Relationship Perspective)** **Depends on how you frame it.** Here’s the rub: - **You’re not TA for:** - **Setting boundaries** (e.g., no junk food, healthier cooking). This is a **healthy household adjustment**. - **Not enabling her dependency** (e.g., refusing to cook what she wants indefinitely). You’re not punishing her; you’re **prioritizing your own health and future**. - **Offering support** (e.g., helping her learn to cook). This shows **collaboration**, not control. - **You *might* be TA for:** - **Assuming she’d automatically adapt** to your changes. You **didn’t discuss the shift** with her—you just **implemented it**. This can feel like **betrayal** (especially given her history with food). - **Not acknowledging her feelings** about the change. Her resistance isn’t "stubbornness"—it’s likely **anxiety** about losing comforts she’s relied on for years. - **Not compromising**. Could you **cook one healthier meal and one "comfort" meal** per day? Or **let her pick a few "treat" meals** per week? --- ### **3. The Core Issue: Power Dynamics** Your relationship has **asymmetrical labor** (you cook, she doesn’t; you drive, she can’t). This imbalance **feeds into her resistance**: - She may feel **powerless** in the kitchen (a space where she historically struggled). - She may **resent the loss of control** over food, which has been a coping mechanism for her. - **Solution:** Frame this as a **team effort**: - *"I’m cooking healthier because I want us to feel better together. Can we figure out a way for you to enjoy it too?"* - *"I’ll help you learn to make your favorite meals—what’s one dish you’d like to try?"* --- ### **4. The "AITA" Verdict: <0.5/1>** **Not fully TA, but not fully justified either.** - **0/1** would be if you **ignored her feelings entirely** and **demanded** she eat what you cook. - **1/1** would be if you **never made changes** and **enabled her unhealthy habits** indefinitely. - **Your score: ~0.5** because: - You’re **making progress** (cooking healthier, exercising). - But you’re **not addressing her emotional resistance** or **compromising enough**. --- ### **How to Improve the Situation** 1. **Have a Direct Conversation:** - *"I love you and want us to be healthy together. I’ve been cooking differently, but I realize it’s been a big change for you. Can we find a middle ground?"* - Ask: *"What’s one small thing you’d be willing to try?"* (e.g., a salad with her favorite dressing, a 10-minute walk). 2. **Reintroduce "Treat" Foods:** - Let her **choose one "cheat" meal per week** (e.g., her favorite takeout) to ease into change. 3. **Make It Fun:** - Turn meals into **experiments** ("Let’s try this new recipe together!"). - Use **small rewards** (e.g., "If we both try the new dish, we’ll watch a movie"). 4. **Address the Underlying Anxiety:** - If her resistance stems from **fear of failure** (e.g., "I’ll gain weight back"), reassure her: *"This is a journey, not a race. We’ll adjust as we go."* 5. **Seek Professional Help if Needed:** - If her **food dependency** is a deeper issue, a **nutritionist or therapist** could help her **rebuild healthy habits** without feeling deprived. --- ### **Final Thought** You’re **not TA for prioritizing your health**, but you **are TA for not considering her feelings** in the process. Relationships thrive on **mutual effort and empathy**—even when one person is making the first move. **A small adjustment (e.g., compromise on meals) could make a huge difference in her buy-in.** Would you like help drafting a script for the conversation?
